_readme: All game content lives here. Anything marked PLACEHOLDER was invented to make the skeleton playable and should be rewritten. Condition syntax used everywhere (appears_when, when, condition): a list of terms that must ALL hold; a term 'a|b' holds if ANY of a or b is active; an empty list or ['any'] always holds. Indicator ids: reach, burden, fiscal, political. Equity is NOT an effect column: it is computed as 100 minus the gap between the best- and worst-served target group, so to move Equity use group_multipliers (on options) or group_reach (on modifiers and cards).

setting.transition_warning: Transition warning: applications already in the pipeline were decided under the old rule. Expect one quarter of mixed outcomes. (PLACEHOLDER wording)
setting.purpose_template: Statement of Purpose. The {program} rests on the {council}'s finding that {cs}. Its governing aim is {gg}, pursued chiefly through {il}. The design draws on {brief}.
setting.purpose_template_lite: Statement of Purpose. The {program} rests on the {council}'s finding that {cs}. Its governing aim is {gg}, pursued chiefly through {il}.
setting.clause_template: A household is eligible if it {trigger} and its income {income_period} is below {threshold} of area median income{residence}.

groups.name: Working families with an eviction notice
Undocumented or mixed-status households
groups.construction: deviants in the political frame: no power

indicators.name: Reach
indicators.description: Share of eligible households that actually receive aid

indicators.name: Burden
indicators.description: Learning, compliance and psychological cost borne by applicants (higher is worse)

indicators.name: Equity
indicators.description: 100 minus the gap between the best- and worst-served target group

indicators.name: Fiscal integrity
indicators.description: Inverse of improper payments and cost overrun

indicators.name: Political support
indicators.description: Council and press standing; renewal odds

full.label: Full (three acts, four quarters, about 50 minutes)

macro.note: Locked after adoption; one reopening offered in the Q3 briefing if indicators are poor, at political cost.

meso.note: Changeable only in the Q2 adjustment phase, at political cost per change.

micro.note: Changeable in any quarter's adjustment phase at no political cost.

choices.name: Causal story
choices.prompt: What kind of problem is this?

options.label: Market failure
options.tooltip: Rents outran wages. Nobody did anything wrong; the market just stopped clearing for the bottom third. You'll want money in the system, not rules.
options.purpose: rents have outrun wages and the rental market no longer clears for low-income households

options.label: Landlord behavior
options.tooltip: Filings are up because filing is cheap and profitable. If the problem is landlord behavior, you're going to want teeth.
options.purpose: opportunistic eviction filings by landlords are driving displacement

options.label: Tenant behavior
options.tooltip: Payment habits, information gaps, people who don't know help exists. Fix the household and the filings follow.
options.purpose: household payment habits and information gaps leave tenants exposed to eviction

options.label: Structural shortage
options.tooltip: There aren't enough units. Any program that pays rent is treating a symptom, and the Q3 briefing will say so.
options.purpose: the city does not have enough affordable units and every rental program treats a symptom

choices.name: Governance goal
choices.prompt: What is the general idea that should govern the program?

options.label: Housing stability as a right
options.tooltip: Nobody gets evicted for want of a few months' rent. Expect the Budget Office to ask what 'nobody' costs.

options.label: Market stabilization
options.tooltip: Keep landlords renting and tenants paying. Both sides of the ledger matter; the people in between matter less.
options.purpose: stabilizing the rental market for landlords and tenants alike

options.label: Fiscal prudence
options.tooltip: Spend only what is needed, only on those who qualify, and be able to prove it. The Tenant Coalition will not like this one.

options.label: Neighborhood preservation
options.tooltip: Keep Rosario Heights looking like Rosario Heights. Works best with neighborhood partners; worst with a portal.
options.purpose: preserving the city's neighborhoods and the people who live in them

choices.name: Instrument logic
choices.prompt: What kind of government response fits the problem?

options.label: Coercive / regulatory
options.tooltip: Rules, duties, penalties. Clear and enforceable, and every stakeholder card will be a complaint.

options.label: Financial / market
options.tooltip: Pay for the outcome you want. Fast, legible, and the auditor's favorite place to look.

options.label: Communicative / voluntary
options.tooltip: Information, persuasion, hotlines. Cheap and gentle. Pairing this with audits and clawbacks confuses everyone, including us.

options.label: Network / co-production
options.tooltip: Work through the nonprofits and tenant groups that already know these households. Trust goes up; paperwork goes down; the audit trail thins.
options.purpose: partnerships with community organizations that co-produce the program

choices.name: Objectives
choices.prompt: Pick two quantified objectives. Any pair creates a tension.

options.label: Cut evictions 30%
options.tooltip: The headline the Mayor wants. Needs money to move fast and landlords to accept it.

options.label: Reach 70% of eligible households
options.tooltip: Take-up is the whole game here. Every form field is an enemy of this objective.

options.label: Improper payments under 3%
options.tooltip: The Budget Office's objective. Every form field is a friend of this one.

options.label: Stabilize small-landlord receipts
options.tooltip: Keep the three-unit owners from selling to the big operators. Serves contenders; the press will notice who gets paid.

options.label: Process applications within 14 days
options.tooltip: Speed. Works against every review step you add downstream.

choices.name: Instrument mix
choices.prompt: How does the money (or the message) move?
choices.note: PLACEHOLDER effects and multipliers; only direction is from the design document

options.label: Direct-to-landlord payment
options.tooltip: Pay the landlord, close the case. Landlords love it, tenants never see the money, and the mixed-status families won't apply if the landlord has to sign.

options.label: Payment to tenant
options.tooltip: Pay the household. Dignity and flexibility; also the occasional payment that never reaches the landlord.

options.label: Conditional (payment + counseling)
options.tooltip: Rent plus a mandatory session with a housing counselor. Changes behavior, if you believe behavior was the problem; adds an appointment nobody asked for.

options.label: Hortatory (campaign + hotline + small grants)
options.tooltip: Bus ads, a hotline and emergency grants. Cheap and visible. Information alone does not pay anyone's rent.

options.label: City housing department
options.tooltip: Our own people. They know the rules and they are already behind on last year's program.

options.label: Community nonprofits
options.tooltip: The organizations the Okafor-Mendez family already trusts. Reach goes up where we need it most; the paper trail gets thinner.

options.label: Private contractor
options.tooltip: Fast, measurable, paid per completed case. Guess which cases they complete first.

options.label: Online portal only
options.tooltip: Cheapest by far. Harold B., 74, does not own a smartphone.

choices.name: Income threshold
choices.prompt: Who is poor enough to qualify?

options.label: 50% AMI
options.tooltip: The poorest third. Tight targeting; many working families with a notice in hand will be just over the line.

options.label: 80% AMI
options.tooltip: The conventional line. Nobody will praise it and nobody will attack it.

options.label: 120% AMI
options.tooltip: Nearly universal. Reach goes up; the Budget Office will ask why a nurse is getting rent money.

choices.name: Benefit cap per month
choices.prompt: How much per household per month?

options.label: Low
options.tooltip: Covers rent in Castelldefels Flats, not in Bayside Terrace. Stretches the budget; leaves some households still short.

options.label: Mid
options.tooltip: Covers the median rent. Fine.

options.label: High
options.tooltip: Covers any rent in the city. Fewer households served, each fully; landlords in the Old Port are delighted.

options.label: 3 months
options.tooltip: A bridge. Households come back in Q+1 if nothing else changed.

options.label: 6 months
options.tooltip: Half a year of stability. The usual.

options.label: 12 months
options.tooltip: A year. Fewer households, more stability each; the auditor will ask about month ten.

options.label: Rolling
options.tooltip: Apply any day. Easy for applicants, hard to budget.

options.label: Two fixed rounds
options.tooltip: Two deadlines a year. Easy to budget; the eviction hearing does not wait for the next round.

choices.name: Eligibility route
choices.prompt: Who can start an application, and in what order are they served?
choices.note: PLACEHOLDER. This setting is not in the Section 4 table; it was added so the Section 5 modifiers and the Section 6 cards that mention 'universal', 'priority tiers' and 'landlord-initiated' eligibility have something to point at.

options.label: Universal (any at-risk household)
options.tooltip: Anyone who says they are at risk may apply. Simple to explain; the line is long.

options.label: Priority tiers
options.tooltip: Serve the most urgent first: hearing date, children, age. Fair on paper; the tiering itself takes a review step.

options.label: Written eviction notice required
options.tooltip: A notice in hand proves need. Also means we help only after the landlord has already started.

options.label: Landlord-initiated
options.tooltip: The landlord applies for the tenant. Fast, bundled, popular with the association. The tenant who never hears about it is not counted anywhere.

choices.name: Documentation
choices.prompt: What must an applicant prove, and how?
choices.note: Effects from Section 5 of the design document. Equity column is expressed as group_multipliers (PLACEHOLDER values).

options.label: Self-attestation
options.tooltip: Sign here that it's true. Everyone finishes the form; some of them should not have.

options.label: Standard
options.tooltip: Lease, ID, one proof of income. The form every other city uses.

options.label: Full verification
options.tooltip: We've caught every fraud case we've ever had this way. We've also lost about a third of applicants before they finish the form.

choices.name: Enforcement posture
choices.prompt: When do we check, and what happens if we were wrong?

options.label: Trust and audit
options.tooltip: Pay first, sample later. Fast money, and the auditor's sample will find something.

options.label: Pre-payment review
options.tooltip: Every file reviewed before a dollar moves. Clean books; the eviction hearing is in eleven days.

options.label: Post-payment clawback
options.tooltip: Pay fast, then send letters demanding money back from anyone who was wrong. One of those letters will go to a data-entry error.

choices.name: Form length
choices.prompt: One page or the full packet?

options.label: One page
options.tooltip: Fits on one side. Some questions we would have liked to ask go unasked.

options.label: Full packet
options.tooltip: Eleven pages and a checklist. Nothing goes unasked; a lot goes unanswered.

choices.name: Appeal window
choices.prompt: Can a denied applicant appeal, and for how long?

options.label: No appeal
options.tooltip: A decision is a decision. Saves staff time; the news story writes itself.

options.label: 14 days
options.tooltip: Two weeks to object. Reasonable.

options.label: 60 days
options.tooltip: Two months to object. Fair, slow, and the caseload never quite closes.

evidence_briefs.author: Messiland Budget Office
evidence_briefs.label: Budget Office cost study
evidence_briefs.text: Every dollar of rental aid displaces 0.8 dollars of private payment. Improper-payment rates in comparable cities ran 6 to 11 percent. Recommends verification before payment. (PLACEHOLDER text)

evidence_briefs.author: Tenant Coalition of Messiland
evidence_briefs.label: Tenant Coalition survey
evidence_briefs.text: Of 600 households surveyed in Rosario Heights and the Old Port, 41 percent did not know aid existed and 28 percent would not apply if a landlord had to sign. Recommends outreach through trusted organizations. (PLACEHOLDER text)

evidence_briefs.author: University administrative-data analysis
evidence_briefs.label: University administrative-data analysis
evidence_briefs.text: Linked court and benefits records show filings concentrated among 40 landlords and 3 neighborhoods. Both the cost and the take-up pictures are visible, but the analysis took a quarter to deliver and Q1 opens with a backlog. (PLACEHOLDER text)

options.text: has received a written eviction notice
, and it has resided in {city} for at least 12 months

fit_rules.explanation: Fiscal prudence, reach 70% and a near-universal threshold cannot all be pursued at once.
A prudence frame with a take-up objective: one of them will give. (PLACEHOLDER)
A rights frame with an error-rate objective pulls the goals column in two directions. (PLACEHOLDER)
Market stabilization and stabilizing landlord receipts are the same goal at two levels.
A rights frame and a take-up objective reinforce each other. (PLACEHOLDER)
You defined the problem as a shortage of units and set an objective a rental program cannot deliver against that story. (PLACEHOLDER)
Co-production, community implementers and trust-based documentation reinforce each other.
A trust-based network with every file reviewed before payment: the means undercut each other.
A communicative logic paired with pre-payment review is inconsistent means.
Persuasion at the top, clawback letters at the bottom. The Tenant Coalition notices first.
A financial logic delivered as direct payment is consistent means.
A regulatory logic delivered through bus ads and a hotline. (PLACEHOLDER)
Co-production through a portal with no partners. (PLACEHOLDER)
Cutting evictions 30% with a hortatory mix: the means cannot deliver the goal.
fit_rules.citation: Van Geet et al. 2021; Schneider & Ingram 1990

fit_rules.explanation: A 70% reach objective paired with full verification is incongruent goal and means.
Reach 70% through a portal only: the groups you most need will not log in. (PLACEHOLDER)
Stabilizing landlord receipts by paying landlords directly: the means fit the goal.
Market stabilization through financial instruments is congruent at the macro level.
An error-rate objective under 3% with self-attested applications. (PLACEHOLDER)
A 14-day processing objective with every file reviewed before payment. (PLACEHOLDER)
A right backed by enforceable duties is congruent at the macro level. (PLACEHOLDER)

modifiers.explanation: Full verification through a portal only: the digital-divide cost falls on the elderly and mixed-status households.
Information alone does not move resource-constrained groups.
Trust networks raise take-up among mixed-status households but thin the audit trail.
Serving contenders: landlords are paid and happy; tenants who were never asked are not served.
Pre-payment review plus priority tiers: the prioritized group waits longest.
The contractor cream-skims the easy cases and leaves the rest to the clawback letters.
The council asks why you are paying the people you said were the problem.
The program cannot fix what it did not aim at: Reach cannot exceed 60.
Inconsistent means: persuasion at the top and clawback letters at the bottom.

cards.title: Marisol R., Rosario Heights
cards.body: Two kids. Eviction hearing in 11 days. Has lease and ID. Her employer pays cash; there is no pay stub.

outcomes.text: Denied: no acceptable proof of income.
Approved on attestation. Payment issued before the hearing.

cards.title: Messiland Ledger, metro section
cards.body: 'Mother of two evicted while city program sat on 60% of its budget.' The article names the documentation rule. Your office is asked for comment.

cards.title: Harold B., 74, Castelldefels Flats
cards.body: Fixed income from Social Security. Income proof is a paper letter. No smartphone, no email.

outcomes.text: Application never completed. Counts against reach for elderly renters.
A volunteer at the neighborhood center completes the form with him.

default.text: Approved after a second visit to the office.

cards.title: The Okafor-Mendez household, the Old Port
cards.body: Mixed status. Three months behind. Afraid to submit anything with a name on it.

outcomes.text: Approved through the parish housing desk. No file leaves the building.

default.text: The household does not apply at all. Silent non-take-up, visible only in Equity.

cards.title: Dana P., owner of three units, Bayside Terrace
cards.body: Two tenants behind. Applies on their behalf with copies of both leases.

outcomes.text: Approved fast. Both arrears paid directly.

default.text: Told the tenants must apply themselves. One does; one never does.

cards.title: Caseworker query: the month-to-month lease
cards.body: Applicant's lease expired last month; she is month-to-month. The rule says 'current lease.' The caseworker asks how to proceed.
cards.reading: Week 7: why designers write policy text

choices.label: Approve
choices.text: Approved; the caseworker notes the interpretation for the file.

choices.label: Deny
choices.text: Denied under a strict reading of 'current lease.'

choices.label: Request a landlord letter (adds 2 weeks)
choices.text: Letter requested. The hearing is in 11 days.

cards.title: Report from a city caseworker
cards.body: To clear the backlog she has been approving self-attested cases under 1,000 USD without review. She asks whether to continue.

choices.label: Endorse it
choices.text: The informal rule continues.

choices.label: Stop it
choices.text: Reviews resume. The backlog grows.

choices.label: Formalize it as a rule
choices.text: A written fast-track for small claims. (Simplified: in the design document this becomes a new setting next quarter.)

cards.title: Contractor's monthly report
cards.body: 94% approval for applications with complete documents, 4% for incomplete ones. Incomplete applications are disproportionately working families and mixed-status households.

default.text: The report is filed. The pattern continues.

cards.title: Letter from the Messiland Landlord Association
cards.body: Offers to pre-screen tenants and submit bundled applications in exchange for direct payment to members.

choices.label: Accept
choices.text: Bundled applications begin arriving the next week.

choices.label: Decline
choices.text: A polite letter back. The association's newsletter is less polite.

choices.label: Accept with a tenant-consent requirement
choices.text: Fewer bundles, each with a signature.

cards.title: Council hearing, Committee on Housing
cards.body: A council member asks why the program has spent 40% of its budget and reached 15% of eligible households.

outcomes.text: 'You built a wall of paper and called it a program.'
'You ran ads.'

default.text: Your deputy answers. The clip is not flattering.

cards.title: City Auditor, sample of 50 payments
cards.body: The auditor finds 3 duplicate payments in the sample.

outcomes.text: Finding published: duplicates paid without review.
No finding. The review queue is now 19 days long.
Letters to 3 households. One was a data-entry error; the Ledger has her name.

cards.title: Plant closure in the Old Port
cards.body: 400 households newly at risk. Applications double next quarter.

outcomes.text: Backlog. The quarter's quota cannot be met.
Quota met. Some of the new approvals will not survive an audit.

cards.title: Notice from the State Housing Fund
cards.body: The state source now requires that recipients be 'legally present.' Your office must respond this quarter.
cards.reading: Stone 2012 ch. 2 on who counts in 'equity'

choices.label: Comply
choices.text: Mixed-status households are no longer eligible.

choices.label: Seek a waiver (one-quarter delay, 50% chance)
choices.text: The request is filed. Payments to affected households pause.

choices.label: Fund mixed-status households from city reserves
choices.text: A separate line in the city budget. The council notices.

cards.title: State Housing Fund: waiver granted
cards.body: The waiver is approved. Paused payments resume with back pay.

cards.title: State Housing Fund: waiver denied
cards.body: The waiver is denied. Mixed-status households lose eligibility, one quarter later than if you had complied.

cards.title: Backlog report
cards.body: After reviews resumed, the queue of unreviewed files passed 300. Average wait is now 26 days.

cards.title: Processing report: priority tiers
cards.body: Every priority-tier file requires a tier review before the pre-payment review. The prioritized group now waits longest.

cards.title: Opening-day backlog
cards.body: The University's analysis took a quarter to deliver. The program opens with 220 applications already waiting from the interim hotline.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER clause ambiguity: 'at risk of eviction'
cards.body: Your clause says 'is at risk of eviction.' A caseworker reads it aloud to a 71-year-old whose landlord has said, verbally, that he is selling the building. No notice, no arrears. Is she at risk?

choices.label: Yes, approve
choices.text: 'At risk' now means what the caseworker says it means.

choices.label: No, deny
choices.text: 'At risk' now means a notice in hand.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER clause ambiguity: income 'at time of application'
cards.body: Your clause measures income 'at time of application.' An applicant lost her job on Tuesday and applied on Wednesday. Her prior-year income was well above the line.

choices.label: Approve: income today is zero
choices.text: Approved. The Budget Office asks how many Tuesdays there are in a year.

choices.label: Deny: use last year's return
choices.text: Denied. The clause now means something it does not say.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER clause ambiguity: 12 months' residence
cards.body: Your clause requires 12 months' residence in the city. A family moved from the county into the Old Port ten months ago. Their utility bills are in a cousin's name.

choices.label: Accept the cousin's bills
choices.text: Approved on the strength of a utility bill in someone else's name.

choices.label: Deny
choices.text: Denied. The family does not reapply.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Ruth and Amadou K., Bayside Terrace
cards.body: Retired couple. Their arrears notice arrived three weeks after the last application deadline.

outcomes.text: The next round opens in nine weeks. The hearing is in four.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Teodoro V., returning applicant
cards.body: Approved last quarter. His aid period ended; his hours were cut again. He is back at the desk.

outcomes.text: A second three-month bridge. The file is now twice as thick.

default.text: Still within his aid period. No action.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Mr. Esposito, one unit above his shop
cards.body: His tenant received aid. The rent has still not arrived.

outcomes.text: The tenant used the money for a car repair to keep her job. The landlord files anyway.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Lucía and her mother, Castelldefels Flats
cards.body: Lucía, 16, is translating the application for her mother at the kitchen table.

outcomes.text: Page seven asks for a document the household does not have. The packet goes in a drawer.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Housing Department staffing memo
cards.body: The department has eleven caseworkers for the program and 1,400 open files. Average processing time is 23 days.

outcomes.text: The 14-day objective is missed by nine days.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Contractor change request
cards.body: The contractor asks to drop the appeal step: 'It adds eight days per file and we are paid per completed case.'

choices.label: Agree
choices.text: Appeals end for contractor-handled files.

choices.label: Refuse
choices.text: The contractor's completion rate drops.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Messiland Ledger asks about the benefit cap
cards.body: A reporter has compared your monthly cap with median rents by neighborhood.

outcomes.text: 'City aid covers two-thirds of the rent in Bayside Terrace.'
'City pays Old Port penthouse rents.'

default.text: The numbers are unremarkable. No story runs.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Council member's amendment
cards.body: A council member proposes requiring two years' city residence for eligibility, 'so Messiland money stays with Messiland families.'

choices.label: Support the amendment
choices.text: The amendment passes committee.

choices.label: Oppose it
choices.text: The amendment fails. The council member remembers.

choices.label: Propose one year instead
choices.text: One year passes.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: State spot audit
cards.body: The state fund audits a random 5% of payments statewide.

outcomes.text: Four improper payments in your sample.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Portal outage
cards.body: The application portal is down for six days during the month's final week.

choices.label: Extend the deadline a week
choices.text: The deadline moves. Budget forecasts slip.

choices.label: Open a paper line at City Hall
choices.text: A line forms on Plaza Diez. The Ledger photographs it.

choices.label: Hold the deadline
choices.text: Those who could not log in do not apply.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Nonprofit caseworker's question
cards.body: A caseworker asks whether she can accept a utility bill as proof of residence for a mixed-status family that has no lease in its own name.

choices.label: Yes
choices.text: Utility bills count. Three more families apply the next week.

choices.label: No
choices.text: The family withdraws.

cards.title: PLACEHOLDER: Small-landlord coalition, public comment
cards.body: Twenty owners of one to four units say they cannot wait for payments and are selling to a regional operator.

outcomes.text: Six buildings sold this quarter.
Direct payment keeps most of them in the market.

evaluators.name: Messiland Budget Office
evaluators.template: Memo from the {evaluator}, after Q{q}. We read the calibrations, not the speeches. Fiscal integrity stands at {fiscal}; applicant burden at {burden}. {verdict} The two files that mattered most this quarter: {cards}. Fit check: {lights}. (PLACEHOLDER template)

verdicts.text: The fine print is holding the line. Resist the pressure to loosen it.
The calibrations leak in places; tighten documentation or enforcement before the next audit.
Money is leaving the building faster than the paperwork can follow it. This is a calibration problem, and it is fixable at your desk.

evaluators.name: Tenant Coalition of Messiland
evaluators.template: Memo from the {evaluator}, after Q{q}. You chose {objectives} as your objectives. Reach stands at {reach}; Equity at {equity}; the worst-served group is {worst_group}. {verdict} Cases we are hearing about on the ground: {cards}. (PLACEHOLDER template)

verdicts.text: The program is reaching the households it was meant for, including the ones that are hardest to reach. Keep the objectives.
The objectives sound right; the tools are not delivering them to groups one through three. Ask who the implementer actually serves.
Whatever this program is for, it is not for the households in Rosario Heights and the Old Port. The objectives were the wrong ones, or the tools cannot reach them.

evaluators.name: Mayor's Chief of Staff
evaluators.template: Memo from the {evaluator}, after Q{q}. Your Statement of Purpose said: "{purpose}" Political support stands at {political}. {verdict} The council remembers: {cards}. Fit check: {lights}. (PLACEHOLDER template)

verdicts.text: The story still holds in council and in the press. The Mayor can run on this.
The story is wobbling. Council members are quoting your own purpose statement back at you. Consider what the frame committed you to.
The frame has not survived contact with the cases. The council is asking whether the problem was ever what you said it was.

evaluators.name: You, as evaluator
evaluators.template: Your own evaluation of Q{q}, through the lens of the {lens_name} ({lens_criterion}). Weighted score {score}. {verdict} Most consequential cards: {cards}. Fit check: {lights}. Compare with the three other evaluators below. (PLACEHOLDER template)

verdicts.text: By this criterion the quarter went well.
By this criterion the quarter was mixed.
By this criterion the quarter went badly.

briefings.title: Council Chamber
briefings.text: From the Mayor: evictions are up 40% year over year. The {council} has declared an emergency and wants a program by the end of the month. The budget is fixed. Before you draft anything, decide what kind of problem this is, what should govern the response, and what kind of instrument fits. Commission one evidence brief; you cannot afford three. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: Drafting Desk
briefings.text: The council adopted your Statement of Purpose. Now set the program's objectives (two, quantified) and choose the instrument mix and the implementer. Every pair of objectives is in tension with itself; the evaluators will find it. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: Fine Print
briefings.text: Settings, calibrations and the eligibility clause. Caseworkers will read your clause aloud to applicants. Whatever it leaves ambiguous becomes their decision, or yours. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: The Ordinance
briefings.text: From the Mayor: evictions are up 40% and the {council} wants the {program} designed by the end of the month. The council has fixed the income threshold, benefit cap, duration and application window; the six choices below are yours. Your causal story will decide what kind of program the council believes it adopted. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: Quarter 1 briefing
briefings.text: The program opens Monday. Applications are arriving at the {mayors_office} and at every neighborhood center. Work the cases. The Budget Office will write the first evaluation. (PLACEHOLDER)
briefings.redesign: Before Q2: the calibrations are yours to change. What did the cases tell you that the design did not?

briefings.title: Quarter 2 briefing
briefings.text: Council review. The {council} will accept changes to objectives and tools this quarter only, and each change costs you standing. Micro settings remain yours. The Tenant Coalition is watching reach by group. (PLACEHOLDER)
briefings.redesign: Before Q3: the meso row is now locked for good. Micro settings remain open.

briefings.title: Quarter 3 briefing
briefings.text: Mid-program. The Chief of Staff wants to know whether the story you told the council in Act 1 still holds. If indicators are poor, the Mayor is willing to reopen the ordinance once, at a cost. (PLACEHOLDER)
briefings.redesign: Before Q4: choose the lens through which you will judge your own final quarter.

briefings.title: Quarter 4 briefing
briefings.text: Final quarter before renewal. You chose your own criterion; the other three evaluators will score the same quarter beside you. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: Quarter 1 briefing
briefings.text: The ordinance passed. The program opens Monday. Work the cases; two evaluators will write after this quarter, one at the level of the fine print and one at the level of your objectives. (PLACEHOLDER)
briefings.redesign: One redesign: documentation and enforcement are yours to change before Q2. Everything else is locked.

briefings.title: Quarter 2 briefing
briefings.text: Second and final quarter. The Mayor's Chief of Staff will judge whether your causal story survived. (PLACEHOLDER)

briefings.title: Quarter 2 briefing
briefings.text: Second and final quarter. The council has delegated the fine print to you: the income threshold and benefit cap are open for one adjustment, alongside documentation and enforcement. The Chief of Staff will judge whether your causal story survived. (PLACEHOLDER)

debrief_prompts: Identify one case where your design produced an outcome you did not intend. Which reading predicted it?
Which evaluator's memo was hardest to dismiss, and what does that tell you about whose criteria you were implicitly designing for?

The game's model assumes certain things about how applicants, caseworkers and landlords behave. Name one such assumption, say whether it is defensible, and say what a real policy designer, or an AI tool, would need to know to check it.

Your fit lights and your indicators probably disagreed at some point. Which would you rather have had, a fitted design or an effective one, and what does the disagreement tell you about the level at which your design went wrong?
